h1: The 7 Best Quiet Printers for Home Offices and Video Calls, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Quiet Home Office Printers: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 quiet home office printers from Epson, Brother, HP and Canon, scored on print mechanism, duplex, feeder and upkeep noise.
summary: The Epson EcoTank ET-4800 is the quiet printer to buy for a shared office, with an ink tank that removes cartridge swaps, an automatic document feeder and an Ethernet port. The ET-2800 is the same idea for a single desk, the Brother Work Smart 1360 adds automatic duplex without a laser's burst of noise, and the HP DeskJet 4355 is the budget pick. The Brother laser models suit people who would rather endure a short loud burst than a long hum.
intro: A quiet printer is not the one with the lowest decibel number on a box. It is the one whose noise arrives at a time and in a pattern you can live with. Inkjets produce a low, steady carriage hum that goes on as long as the page prints, while lasers go silent for a long time and then fire a loud burst as the fuser warms up. Which of those annoys you depends on whether you sit near the printer during calls.

So this ranking sorts printers by how and when they make noise, as well as how often they need maintenance. We reviewed seven models from their listings, comparing the print mechanism, duplex, document feeder, connectivity and upkeep demands such as cartridge swaps. None of the listings gives a measured decibel level, so we rank on mechanism and use, and we say so where a claim is open to doubt.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-4800 Wireless All-in-One Cartridge-Free Supertank Printer
products.verdict: A cartridge-free inkjet with a feeder and Ethernet, built for a shared office that wants fewer interruptions.
products.description:
Epson's ET-4800 swaps cartridges for refillable ink bottles and adds an automatic document feeder, Ethernet alongside wireless, and scan, copy and fax. Its carriage-motor engine is typical of inkjets, and the price lands in the $100 to $200 range.

It wins because noise from a printer is partly about everything around the printing. A cartridge model makes a flurry of clicks, whirs and prime cycles when you swap a cartridge, and an ink tank skips most of that. The feeder means a multi-page scan runs in one pass rather than a page-at-a-time lid routine, which cuts the repeated mechanical noise. Ethernet gives a stable wired link, so the printer doesn't wake up and renegotiate Wi-Fi.

Buy it for a shared quiet office that prints and scans regularly. The caveat is that any carriage inkjet produces a continuous hum while it prints, so it is quiet in the sense of steady, not silent.
pros: Refillable tanks mean no cartridge swaps
Scan, copy and fax built in
cons: Carriage hum lasts through a print
products.idealFor: Shared quiet offices that scan multi-page documents.
products.skipIf: You only print a few pages a month.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-2800 Wireless Color All-in-One Cartridge-Free Supertank Printer
products.verdict: The ink tank formula without the feeder, for a quiet office that prints regularly.
products.description:
Think of the ET-2800 as the ink tank idea stripped to essentials: refillable bottles, scan and copy, wireless, and a carriage-motor engine, all for $100 to $200.

It ranks just behind the ET-4800 because it gives you the same low-fuss ink tank system without the document feeder, Ethernet port or fax. For a single desk that is often enough, since a person who prints a handful of pages a day doesn't need a feeder. Fewer ink-change routines mean fewer moments when the printer clicks and purges, and the compact build suits a bookshelf.

Choose it if you work alone and want steady, low-interruption printing. Skip it if you scan multi-page documents, because the lid scanning is manual and slower.
products.idealFor: Solo home office workers who print daily.
products.skipIf: You regularly scan stacks of pages.

products.name: Brother Work Smart 1360 Wireless Color Inkjet All-in-One Printer
products.verdict: Automatic two-sided printing on an inkjet, with no laser warm-up burst.
products.description:
Brother built the Work Smart 1360 around automatic two-sided printing, then added a small 1.8 inch color screen, wireless and a trial of its Refresh ink plan. It lives in the $100 to $200 range and uses a carriage inkjet engine.

It takes third place because duplex printing is a noise topic of its own. Flipping a page makes extra mechanical sounds, but doing it automatically on an inkjet keeps the pattern even and avoids the sudden spool-up of a laser. The small display also makes setup and troubleshooting easier without hunting through an app. It ranks below the Epson tank models since it uses cartridges, so you will face cartridge swaps more often.

Buy it if you print double-sided documents and want to avoid a laser's burst. The caveat is that the subscription program is an optional extra, and cartridge ink costs more per page.
products.idealFor: Double-sided printing in a quiet home office.
products.skipIf: You want to avoid cartridge changes altogether.

products.name: HP DeskJet 4355 Wireless All-in-One Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: A compact, low-cost inkjet with a steady hum, best near video calls when printing is light.
products.description:
HP's DeskJet 4355 is the small, simple option, with print, scan and copy, easy wireless setup and a 3-month Instant Ink trial. A carriage inkjet engine drives it, and it costs $50 to $100.

It ranks fourth because it delivers the quiet pattern of a carriage inkjet at the lowest cost here. For a desk near a camera, a lower and steadier hum is easier on the ear than a sudden burst, and this printer's small size keeps it out of the way. The tradeoff is a cartridge system, so the ink runs out faster and each swap makes noise, and it has no feeder or duplex.

Pick it if you print a few pages a week and want to spend as little as possible. Skip it if you print every day, because ink cost and cartridge swaps will wear on you.
products.idealFor: Light printing at a desk near video calls.
products.skipIf: You print more than a few pages each day.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TR4720 All-in-One Wireless Printer
products.verdict: A cheap inkjet with an automatic document feeder for quiet multi-page scanning.
products.description:
Canon's PIXMA TR4720 pairs an auto document feeder with a moving-carriage inkjet engine, then adds mobile printing, wireless and a legacy fax line. Expect to spend $50 to $100.

It ranks fifth because it gives you a feeder at a price where rivals offer none. Feeding a stack through once is quieter and quicker than lifting a lid for every page, so a home office that scans receipts and contracts benefits. It trails the Epson ET-2800 because it uses cartridges, and its fax function is a legacy feature most people will never touch.

Buy it if you scan multi-page documents often on a small budget. Skip it if you print heavily, where cartridge refills will cost more than an ink-tank machine.
cons: Cartridge ink is costly over time
products.idealFor: Quiet offices that scan multi-page documents regularly.
products.skipIf: You print many pages each week.

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW Wireless Compact Monochrome Multi-Function Laser Printer
products.verdict: A compact mono laser with duplex that prints in a short, loud burst and then goes quiet.
products.description:
Brother's DCP-L2640DW squeezes copy, scan and automatic duplex into a compact black-and-white laser, with wireless, mobile printing and Alexa support. A fuser and drum do the work, and it costs $200 to $500.

It ranks sixth because laser noise is a different shape from inkjet noise. A fuser needs to heat up, which creates a short burst of fan and gear sound, but afterwards the printer sits silent for long stretches. People who take calls near the printer may prefer that to a long hum. It is black-and-white only and costs more up front.

Choose it if you print occasionally, mostly text, and prefer short noise to long noise. Skip it if you need color or a feeder.
products.idealFor: Occasional text printing where short bursts beat long hums.

products.name: Brother HL-L3220CDW Color Laser Printer
products.verdict: A color laser with duplex and a 250-sheet tray, for the burst-then-silence pattern in color.
products.description:
The HL-L3220CDW is Brother's color laser for small offices, rated at 19 pages per minute with automatic duplex, a 250-sheet tray, and wireless and mobile printing. Its fuser and drum engine puts it at $200 to $500.

It ranks last because it is a print-only machine with no scanner, and the color laser warm-up adds to the burst. The advantage is the same burst-then-silence behavior as the mono laser, but with color documents, and a large tray that means fewer paper reloads. At 19 pages per minute, jobs finish quickly, which shortens the noisy period.

Buy it if you need color documents and want laser behavior. Skip it if you need to scan or copy, since this model does neither.
products.idealFor: Offices that print color documents in short runs.

methodology.title: Print mechanism and noise pattern
methodology.description: We compared carriage inkjets, which hum steadily, with fuser-and-drum lasers, which are silent between jobs but loud at warm-up.

methodology.title: Maintenance interruptions
methodology.description: Cartridge swaps, ink priming and refilling were weighed, since they are among the loudest moments for an inkjet.

methodology.title: Duplex and document feeding
methodology.description: Automatic duplex and feeder trays were scored for how they reduce manual handling and repeated mechanical noise.

methodology.title: Connectivity
methodology.description: Ethernet and wireless links were compared for stability, since a printer that reconnects often wakes up more often.

methodology.title: Value across budgets
methodology.description: Features were set against the $50 to $100, $100 to $200 and $200 to $500 buckets that make up this guide.

whatMatters.detail: Inkjets move a carriage across the page, producing a steady hum for as long as the job runs. Lasers heat a fuser and spin a drum, so they are loud for a moment and then silent. Decide which pattern disturbs you less, then match it to your calls and desk position.

Changing a cartridge causes clicks, purges and a priming cycle, and a cartridge printer does it often. An ink tank printer refills from bottles and skips most of that. Look for the word cartridge-free or ink tank in the listing.

Automatic duplex handles a page twice inside the machine, which adds sound but saves your attention. A document feeder lets a multi-page scan run in one pass. Check the listing for the exact words automatic duplex and auto document feeder, because some models only offer manual duplex.

A printer that drops off Wi-Fi often has to wake and reconnect, which brings extra noise and a failed first print. Ethernet gives the steadiest link, as on the Epson ET-4800. If you rely on wireless, place the printer within a good signal range.

A shelf, a cabinet or a hard desk will each carry vibration differently. A printer on a hollow surface amplifies hum, while a rubber mat or a shelf separated from your desk softens it. Decide on the location before you pick a model, since placement changes perceived noise as much as the mechanism.

cards.label: Ink tank
cards.text: You refill from bottles, so there are fewer swaps and purges and a lower running cost. Picks: Epson ET-4800 and ET-2800.

cards.label: Cartridge inkjet
cards.text: Cheaper to buy but costlier to run, with more frequent swaps that add noise. Picks: HP DeskJet 4355, Canon TR4720, Brother Work Smart 1360.

howToChoose.note: Default to an ink tank if you print weekly, and a cartridge model if you print rarely.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A printer that makes noise on your terms: a quiet steady inkjet you can ignore, or a laser you only run between calls. Keep it off the desk surface and away from your microphone.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Epson ET-2800 for a steady hum at a single desk, or the Brother DCP-L2640DW when you can print between meetings.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You print weekly, share the printer, or need color laser. The Epson ET-4800 and Brother HL-L3220CDW are the picks for heavier use.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You print occasionally and want a basic scanner. The HP DeskJet 4355 or Canon TR4720 will do.

faq.q: Do any of these printers have a quiet mode?
faq.a: The listings do not mention one, so we do not claim it. Many printers offer a quiet setting in their software that slows printing to reduce noise, so check the settings menu after setup.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake when buying a quiet printer?
faq.a: Chasing a decibel figure without thinking about the pattern. A printer that hums for two minutes can bother you more than one that bursts for twenty seconds. Choose based on how your calls and desk are arranged.

faq.q: Is an ink tank printer worth it over a cheaper inkjet?
faq.a: If you print weekly, yes. Tanks refill from bottles at a lower cost per page and avoid frequent cartridge swaps. For occasional printing, a cheaper cartridge model costs less overall.

faq.q: How do I set up a wireless printer?
faq.a: Plug in the printer, follow the on-screen prompts to join your Wi-Fi network, and install the maker's app on your phone or computer. Place the printer within good signal range of your router.

faq.q: How can I reduce printer noise without buying a new one?
faq.a: Set the printer on a soft mat or a separate shelf, use a quiet setting if available, and print drafts at normal quality instead of best quality. Vibration through a hollow desk makes a printer sound louder.

faq.q: Do lasers run hotter and louder than inkjets?
faq.a: Lasers run warmer because the fuser heats paper, and they make a sharp burst at warm-up. They are then silent between jobs. Inkjets stay cooler but hum while printing.

finalTake: The Epson EcoTank ET-4800 is the best quiet printer for a shared home office, with a cartridge-free tank, a feeder and Ethernet. The ET-2800 suits one desk, the Brother Work Smart 1360 adds quiet duplex, and the HP DeskJet 4355 is the budget choice. If you prefer a short loud burst and then silence, take a Brother laser instead.
